Living things are not confined to the familiar temperate realm of land, water, and sunlight inhabited by plants and plant-eating animals. They can be found in the darkest depths of the ocean, in hot volcanic mud, in pools beneath the frozen surface of the Antarctic, and buried kilometers deep in the Earth's crust. The creatures that live in these extreme environments are generally unfamiliar, not only because they are inaccessible, but also because they are mostly microscopic. In more homely habitats, too, most organisms are too small for us to see without special equipment: they tend to go unnoticed, unless they cause a disease or rot the timbers of our houses. Yet microorganisms make up most of the total mass of living matter on our planet. Only recently, through new methods of molecular analysis and specifically through the analysis of DNA sequences, have we begun to get a picture of life on Earth that is not grossly distorted by our biased perspective as large animals living on dry land.
① The Hidden Majority of Life on Earth
② The Secret Lives of Animals on Dry Land
③ Why Extreme Habitats Remain the Last Frontier of Animal Evolution
④ How DNA Analysis Confirmed the Superiority of Traditional Biology
⑤ The Limited Role of Microscopic Life in Earth's Ecosystems

The idea of music direction, in the sense of someone shaping and leading a musical performance, goes back to the beginnings of music. Even the gamelans of ancient Indonesia had leaders who would signal to the group changes of meter and tempo, beginnings and endings, and transitions from piece to piece. Yet listening audiences are rarely aware of any musical leadership, and for good aesthetic reason. They need not be aware to fulfill their experience; indeed, the unnecessarily conspicuous presence of a musical leader will detract from it. An audience is better off, for the most part, taking in the whole of a stage work rather than being party to the techniques that go into realizing it. This is not to say that when an orchestra plays alone the audience members' eyes are not fixed on the conductor for the majority of the time; they probably are. When music is accompanying something happening on stage, however, all eyes turn to the stage, and so do everyone's ears, too (including the music director's).

④ Only highly trained listeners are capable of grasping a stage work as a unified artistic whole.

According to Peter Drucker's Post-Capitalist Society, the real, controlling resource and absolutely vital "factor of production" nowadays is neither capital nor land nor labor. ( ① ) The basic economic resource is and will continue to be knowledge. The traditional "factors of production" — land, labor and capital — have not disappeared, but they have become secondary. ( ② ) And knowledge in this new sense means knowledge as a unity, knowledge as the means to obtain social and economic results. ( ③ ) That knowledge has become the resource, rather than a resource. Knowledge is what makes our society "post-capitalist." It creates new social and economic dynamics as well as new politics. In order to achieve success in the long-term, policy must be directed at converting manufacturing from a labor-based enterprise into a knowledge-based one. ( ④ ) The fact that the market economy organizes economic activity around information is what makes it superior. Neither the allocation of capital to productive uses nor labor — the two vehicles of 19th- and 20th-century economic growth — will be the central creators of wealth. ( ⑤ ) Value is now created by "productivity" and "innovation," both of which are applications of knowledge to work. The economic challenge of the post-capitalist society will therefore be the productivity of knowledge work and the knowledge worker.

We are a species that delights in story. We look out on reality, we grasp patterns, and we join them into narratives that can captivate, inform, amuse, and thrill. The plural — narratives — is utterly essential. In the library of human reflection, there is no single, unified volume that conveys ultimate understanding. Instead, we have written many stories that study different domains of human inquiry and experience: stories, that is, that divide and analyze the patterns of reality using different grammars and vocabularies. Protons, neutrons, and electrons are essential for telling the story of elements, analyzing the stuff of reality. Metabolism, mutation, and adaptation are essential for telling the story of life's emergence and development, analyzing the biochemical workings of remarkable molecules and cells. Neurons, information, and awareness are essential for the story of mind — and with that the narratives proliferate: myth to religion, literature to philosophy, art to music, telling of humankind's struggle for survival, will to understand, urge for expression, and search for meaning. *proliferate: 증식하다
① There is no absolute truth; all knowledge is purely subjective.
② Every field of study is ultimately explained by a unified theory of nature.
③ We tend to organize knowledge in narrative forms that are easy to remember.
④ We need various disciplines to explain the world and ourselves.
⑤ We are conditioned to link diverse physical phenomena to one single concept.
